羊角號是古代中東猶太禮儀用的氣鳴角，見於希伯來聖經、塔木德與拉比文獻。早期除在聖: The shofar is an aerophone horn used in the ritual of the ancient Middle East, and it appears in the Hebrew Bible, the Talmud and rabbinic literature. In earlier times it was used in Temple ritual alongside the trumpet, and also to announce the new moon, the Jubilee, war and processions. In later periods it was blown mainly at the Jewish New Year, at the end of Yom Kippur and on weekdays in the month of Elul; during the diaspora, because of the ban on instruments, it became a symbol of mourning for the destruction of the Temple, and the practice arose of nine blasts, or three sets of blasts, at the New Year.
羊角號是古代樂器號角，通常以公羊角製成，屬氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sac: The shofar is an ancient instrument of the horn kind, usually made from a ram's horn; it is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 423.121.2. Like a modern horn it has no device for changing pitch, and the pitch is controlled entirely by the player's lips and embouchure. Depending on the animal chosen and how much it is worked, the instrument varies in size and shape. It is used in Jewish ritual, blown in the synagogue at the New Year and at the end of Yom Kippur, and also on weekday mornings in the month of Elul. Its region is given as the Middle East.
羊角號的發聲體與琴身主要為動物角，通常取公羊角；依來源所載，牛科動物的角可用，但: The sounding body and the body of the shofar are mainly an animal horn, usually a ram's; according to the source, the horns of bovids may be used, except those of cattle. In the ritual of the Jerusalem Temple the principal instrument at the New Year was a wild goat's horn, straighter in shape and with a gold-mounted mouthpiece, while for the fast day a curved ram's horn was used, with a silver-mounted mouthpiece. It has no device for altering pitch, the pitch being controlled by the player's embouchure; it is an aerophone from the Middle East, Hornbostel–Sachs number 423.121.2. The materials of its other parts are not stated in the source.
羊角號音色粗獷而富有穿透力，帶有明亮且略帶刺激的金屬感，具有原始而神聖的氣質。其: The shofar's timbre is rough and penetrating, with a bright, slightly abrasive metallic quality and an air both primitive and sacred. Its range is limited, lying mainly in the middle and upper register, and the number of notes is restricted by the instrument's construction. Its resonance depends mainly on the natural resonance of the horn's inner space, which gives the timbre a warm, natural foundation. Compared with modern brass instruments, the shofar's tone is coarser and more organic, lacking fine control of colour, and precisely for that reason it gives out a bleak, solemn mood. Its tone lies somewhere between the trombone and a shepherd's pipe, with a strong national and religious character; it carries through space, and is especially expressive out of doors.
